A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable text, figures, tables, and appendices. Existing content can be matched across the added appendix and subsequent renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of reasoning length against counting accuracy, grade-prediction error, puzzle-solving accuracy, and safety-related responses, including extensive appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original empirical results and adds experiments using natural-language distractors and explicit or implicit priors in grade prediction.

M1.justification: The controlled, natural, and cautioned overthinking procedures remain unchanged. No model architecture, training objective, or reasoning-control algorithm is revised; Appendix G extends the evaluation scenarios.

E1.justification: New Appendix G adds counting problems with fluent, LLM-generated distractors and grade-prediction scenarios containing explicit or implicit predictor priors. These extend input conditions within existing task families; the earlier benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in corresponding existing experiments. Figure 34 evaluates the same nine models already studied. Claude Sonnet 4.5 is introduced as a distractor generator, not an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix G introduces a 200-question realism experiment with five distractors per question. The prior experiments sample 100 zero-shot regression instances and apply three prior phrasings, producing 300 examples per condition. These are new experimental protocols, not replacements for the original settings.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds targeted tests of whether inverse scaling depends on templated distractor language and whether predictor priors mitigate regression failures. Existing distractor-count, few-shot, cautioned-prompting, Simpson’s-paradox, and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A.4 newly explains accuracy intervals as ±1.96 SEM, regression bars as ±SEM, token-cost SEM, and pooling across questions and seeds. v1 already reported confidence intervals, regression SEM, and repetition counts; v2 does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: New Figure 34 reports declining counting accuracy for Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Sonnet 4 with fluent distractors and adds model-specific regression results under both prior conditions. Existing numerical tables, performance curves, correlations, and qualitative examples are retained; revised axis ticks are presentation changes.

T1.justification: No theoretical results, proofs, or substantive formal assumptions are added or revised. The Zebra-puzzle token estimates remain unchanged. The added standard SEM formulas explain statistical reporting rather than introduce new theory.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same inverse-scaling contribution and five failure modes. The introduction clarifies familiar-framing behavior, while the added experiments support existing claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix G interprets persistence with fluent distractors as evidence against a purely synthetic-wording explanation. It also argues that verbal priors can encourage excessive reliance on one feature, contrasting this with the benefits of concrete few-shot examples. The original naturalness limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new distractor-generation prompt, Claude Sonnet 4.5 generator, 16,000-token generation budget, template counts, and prior-construction procedure. Existing hardware, inference libraries, quantization information, and code/data access disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds Hassid et al. (2025) and Ghosal et al. (2025), distinguishing the latter’s injected-token evaluation from natural overthinking. Additional model system-card references support model descriptions and the new generator. The broader research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify framing effects and reasoning-budget compliance, and Appendix A gains explanatory detail. A new Appendix G shifts the former Appendices G–I to H–J. Publication information is added, while the main narrative and section sequence remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds the three-panel Figure 34 and revises horizontal-axis scaling, ticks, and some panel headings across many existing plots. Some figures are relocated or renumbered. The multi-panel designs, table structures, and overall visual organization are retained.

improvement.justification: Appendix G partly addresses v1’s stated naturalness concern and adds useful evidence about sensitivity to predictor priors. Fuller generation and statistical documentation improves auditability. These gains remain limited: the tasks are still constructed, and regression captions still describe 95% confidence intervals while Appendix A specifies SEM.
